works.title: Brandenburg Concertos
works.standfirst: Six concertos sent to Christian Ludwig of Brandenburg, and the work on which every argument about baroque performance style eventually lands.

anchors.listen_for: The harpsichord cadenza — Pinnock plays it as an argument rather than a display, and the ensemble waits on him rather than the reverse.
Two violas alone. Listen for how little vibrato is used to shape the line, and how the phrase still bends.
Concertino and ripieno stay separable throughout; a good test of whether your copy has been compressed.

reception.note: Received as the accessible face of period practice: the set that persuaded listeners who found Harnoncourt astringent.
Settles into the standard library recommendation; the Penguin Guide keeps it in the front rank across editions.
Still cited at the head of surveys, now as much for consistency as for novelty. Pinnock's 2007 remake divides opinion — broader, some say safer.

editions.label: Archiv Produktion
editions.transfer: Original analogue issue.

editions.label: Archiv Produktion
editions.transfer: First CD issue, Nos. 1–3. Early digital transfer of the 1982 tapes.

sources.text: Natural perspective, clear separation of concertino and ripieno, hall resonance well judged.

editions.label: Archiv Produktion
editions.transfer: Concertos coupled with the Orchestral Suites; the widely circulated second-hand set.

sources.text: Same tapes, later mastering; slightly firmer bass, no obvious noise reduction.

editions.label: Avie
editions.transfer: Different recording, not a transfer: European Brandenburg Ensemble, broader tempos.

sources.text: Elegant simplicity, directness of expression and consistency of approach; a leading modern recommendation.
Frequently placed at the head of recent surveys as an HIP benchmark; crisp articulation throughout.
Long-standing recommendation; refined and stylish.
The definitive period-instrument Brandenburgs of our time.
A reference point for clarity and rhythmic vitality among HIP cycles.

recordings.soloists: Alice Harnoncourt, Jürg Schaeftlein, Walter Holy and principals

anchors.listen_for: Hunting horns played as hunting horns — rough, forward, refusing to blend. The whole argument of the cycle is audible in thirty seconds.
Solo violin phrasing shaped by rhetoric rather than line; note where Harnoncourt lifts before a strong beat.
Chamber scale. Four players, no conductor's blend, every entry exposed.

reception.note: Received as provocation. Reviewers split between historical seriousness and complaints of thin, effortful playing.
Becomes the reference point of the early-music argument; imitated widely enough that its roughness stops sounding strange.
Reassessed as a founding document. Praise shifts from the playing itself to what the playing made possible.

editions.label: Telefunken Das Alte Werk
editions.transfer: Original analogue issue.

editions.label: Teldec
editions.transfer: 1992 digital remastering of the 1964 tapes; the common second-hand CD.

sources.text: Dry 1964 analogue; remarkable clarity of inner parts, little hall, limited bass extension.

editions.label: Warner Classics
editions.transfer: Reissued inside Harnoncourt anthology boxes; transfer lineage not yet established.

sources.text: Pioneering period-instrument cycle of enduring value; a foundational document.
Retains pioneering energy and chamber-scale intensity despite dry original sound.

Still regarded as a reference for its pioneering status and austere sonority.

works.title: Symphony No. 5
works.standfirst: Written after the Pravda attack and premiered to a half-hour ovation. Whether the finale is triumph or coercion is the argument, and every recording takes a side.

anchors.listen_for: The two-note descending figure the whole symphony is built from. How heavily it is attacked sets the terms for everything after.
Strings divided into eight parts, no brass at all. The question is whether the conductor lets it be slow enough to become uncomfortable.
The repeated A in the strings under a hammered D major. Whether this reads as triumph or as coercion is the central interpretive argument of the piece, and every recording answers it.

reception.note: Premiered 21 November in Leningrad under Mravinsky; reported ovations of over half an hour. Received officially as rehabilitation after the 1936 Pravda attack.
Established in the West as a repertory symphony. Read largely at face value: a heroic affirmation, sometimes discussed as Soviet neoclassicism.
Volkov's Testimony recasts the finale as forced rejoicing. Its authenticity is disputed; the reading is not. Performance practice divides along this line and has not reconverged.
The BSO/Nelsons cycle brings the work back to prominence on record, winning the 2017 Grammy for Best Orchestral Performance.

editions.label: Deutsche Grammophon
editions.transfer: Original issue, live Symphony Hall recording. Grammy-winning album, coupled with Symphonies 8 and 9 and the Hamlet suite.

sources.source: Grammy — Best Orchestral Performance, 59th Annual Grammy Awards
sources.text: Awarded Best Orchestral Performance for the album containing Symphonies 5, 8 and 9.

anchors.listen_for: Mravinsky premiered the work in 1937. The tempo relationships here are the closest thing on record to a first reading.
The speed of the coda, which Mravinsky treats faster than most Western conductors — a documentary fact in the argument about what the ending means.

reception.note: Mravinsky conducted the premiere and remained associated with the work for four decades.
Successive Leningrad performances circulate on Soviet and Japanese issues; the discography is tangled and poorly documented.
Japanese labels, chiefly Altus, issue restored live performances; edition identification becomes the practical problem for buyers.

editions.label: Altus
editions.transfer: Japanese issue, 44:08. Cover art present in the Cover Art Archive.

editions.label: Altus
editions.transfer: Vienna 1978 live, coupled with Schubert 8. Barcode verified.

editions.label: Praga
editions.transfer: Coupled with Symphony No. 9 under Košler. Barcode verified.

editions.label: Altus
editions.transfer: Tokyo, 26 May 1973, live. Barcode verified; MusicBrainz release not yet matched.

anchors.listen_for: Barbican strings in eight parts, captured in DSD. A test of whether the hall's dry acoustic helps the transparency or thins the tone.
Where this account sits on the triumph-or-coercion question. Compare directly against Mravinsky's faster coda.

reception.note: Issued as part of Noseda's nine-year LSO cycle, completed and boxed as LSO0907 in 2025. Reception of the cycle as a whole has been strong; individual-issue criticism of the Fifth is not yet cited here.

editions.label: LSO Live
editions.transfer: Original issue, coupled with Symphony No. 1. DSD source, also released as 24-bit/96 kHz FLAC.

editions.label: LSO Live
editions.transfer: Complete cycle box, Symphonies 1–15. Same recordings; transfer lineage not yet established.

works.title: Tosca
works.standfirst: Three acts of political violence at close range, and the opera where a recording either has dramatic nerve or has nothing.

recordings.soloists: Maria Callas, Giuseppe Di Stefano, Tito Gobbi
recordings.ensemble: Orchestra e Coro del Teatro alla Scala

anchors.listen_for: Vulnerability and defiance in the same phrase. Listen to where Callas stops singing legato and starts speaking.
Gobbi never raises the pressure by volume. The menace is in the timing of his answers.
De Sabata builds it without letting the chorus swamp Scarpia's line — a balance most stereo remakes lose.

anchors.where: Act II, 'E avanti a lui tremava tutta Roma'
anchors.listen_for: Legge reportedly kept Callas on this one line for half an hour. Judge whether it was worth it.

reception.note: An immediate commercial success and a critical event; praised for dramatic truth at a time when vocal beauty was the usual measure.
Karajan's stereo Tosca arrives and the discussion becomes sound versus performance — a framing the guide still inherits.
Canonised. Appears at or near the top of nearly every opera survey; the mono limitation is treated as a price worth paying.
Remastering becomes the live question. Which transfer you own now matters more than whether to own it.

editions.label: Columbia
editions.transfer: Original mono issue.

editions.label: EMI
editions.transfer: Great Recordings of the Century series; earlier-generation digital transfer.

sources.text: Mono. Legge's balance places the voices in a real theatre space; dynamic range limited by 1953 tape.

editions.label: Warner Classics
editions.transfer: Callas Remastered: new 24-bit transfers from original tapes.

sources.text: Fresh transfer from original tapes; more air at the top and less congestion in ensembles.

editions.label: Pristine Audio
editions.transfer: XR reprocessing; a different philosophy of restoration, and divisive on principle.

sources.text: Ambient reprocessing adds space that was never recorded. Rewards or falsifies, depending on your view.
Universally regarded as the dramatic benchmark; the Act II confrontation remains unmatched.
The greatest Tosca recording for many critics; a recording of permanent reference value.
The legendary 1953 recording — one of the greatest opera recordings ever made.
Landmark mono recording whose dramatic immediacy has never been surpassed.
Benchmark status confirmed across decades of critical writing.

recordings.soloists: Leontyne Price, Giuseppe Di Stefano, Giuseppe Taddei

anchors.listen_for: Culshaw's staging: bells and chorus placed in depth, Scarpia forward. Stereo used dramatically, not decoratively.
Price shapes it in long breaths where Callas breaks it into speech. The clearest illustration of two whole traditions.
Vienna Philharmonic strings and Karajan's patience with orchestral sonority — the moment his critics and admirers both point at.

reception.note: Welcomed as the modern Tosca the catalogue needed: stereo, and vocally distinguished enough to stand beside 1953.
Holds its place as the stereo recommendation; Taddei's Scarpia gains admirers over time.
Reassessed upward for engineering. Frequently cited as a demonstration of what Decca's team could do in 1962.

editions.label: Decca
editions.transfer: Original stereo issue.

sources.text: Culshaw and Parry at the Sofiensaal: wide stage, natural perspective, firm orchestral definition.

editions.label: Decca
editions.transfer: 96 kHz / 24-bit transfer; the standard modern CD.

sources.text: 24-bit transfer preserves the stage; a small lift in level over earlier CD issues.

editions.label: Pristine Audio
editions.transfer: Stereo XR remastering by Andrew Rose.

sources.text: XR remastering; tighter bass, brighter top, and the usual argument about whether that is the tape or the engineer.
Outstanding stereo alternative; Price sensuous and opulent, Karajan flexible and powerful.
The finest stereo Tosca for many listeners; complementary to the de Sabata set.
